name: ArcticDB
license: Business Source License 1.1 (source-available, not OSI open source): free for non-commercial, personal and academic use, while any business use, even in research or development, needs a commercial licence. Each version becomes Apache 2.0 two years after its release; 1.0 converted in March 2025
summary: Man Group’s serverless DataFrame database: a Python library with a C++ engine that stores versioned pandas DataFrames directly in S3, Azure Blob Storage or local LMDB.
intro: ArcticDB has no server. It is a Python package whose C++ engine turns pandas DataFrames, Series and NumPy arrays into its own columnar format, slices them by rows and by columns, compresses the pieces and writes them straight to S3-compatible object storage, Azure Blob Storage or LMDB on local disk. Each dataset is a symbol inside a library, and symbols share nothing, so many clients can work on different symbols in parallel and capacity grows with the storage rather than a cluster. Frames can be wide as well as long: Man Group says one symbol can hold a 20-year history of more than 400,000 securities, and its launch announcement spoke of hundreds of thousands of columns.

Every `write`, `append` or `update` creates a new version instead of changing data in place. Storage is layered: a mutable reference key points to the latest version, versions form an immutable linked list, each version points to a B-tree index, and the index points to immutable data segments, so unchanged segments are shared between versions. Reading with `as_of` returns a symbol as it was at an earlier version or time, and a snapshot names the current version of many symbols at once. Reads filter by date range and columns, and a lazy, pandas-like API pushes filters and aggregations into the C++ engine; results come back as pandas, Arrow or Polars. There is no SQL.

Man Group built ArcticDB for its quant researchers and runs its front-office time-series analysis on it, and Bloomberg integrated it into its BQuant platform after a 2023 agreement. The source is on GitHub, but under the BSL any business use needs a paid licence from ArcticDB Limited until a version turns Apache 2.0, two years after it ships.
strengths: No server to run: `pip install arcticdb` and point it at a bucket or a local folder
Versions and time travel by default, plus multi-symbol snapshots for reproducible research and backtests
Handles frames that are huge in both directions: billions of rows, hundreds of thousands of columns
Pandas in, pandas out, with filtering and aggregation run in a multi-threaded C++ engine
limits: Source-available, not open source: business use, even for research or development, needs a commercial licence until a version converts
No transactions or isolation: concurrent writers to one symbol are last-writer-wins, so applications must coordinate them or use staged writes
Each write keeps a version, so storage grows; Man’s enterprise tools add pruning and compaction

snippet.title: Write, append, slice and time-travel a symbol
source: lib.write("EURUSD", df)            # version 0 (df has a DatetimeIndex)
lib.append("EURUSD", next_day_df)  # version 1; must start after the last row
# a date range and two columns, read straight from object storage
before = lib.read("EURUSD", as_of=0).data  # as it was before the append
lib.snapshot("eod-2026-10-06")             # pin every symbol’s current version

story: Man Group, a quantitative investment firm, began building Arctic in 2012: a Python datastore for time series and tick data that kept pandas DataFrames in MongoDB. It underpinned Man’s research and trading from its first release, was open-sourced on GitHub in 2015 under the LGPL, and went on to more than a million downloads.

In 2018 Man started a ground-up rewrite to get past Arctic’s limits. ArcticDB dropped MongoDB for ordinary S3-compatible storage, moved the engine to C++ for an order-of-magnitude speedup, and kept Arctic’s pandas-centred Python API. In February 2023 Man signed a multi-year development agreement with Bloomberg, which built ArcticDB into BQuant, its analytics platform for quants. Version 1.0 shipped in March 2023 under the Business Source License, with a paid licence for production use.

Arctic is now in maintenance mode, and ArcticDB has shipped steadily since, reaching the 6.x series in 2026. Because each version’s licence turns into Apache 2.0 after two years, 1.0 became Apache 2.0 on March 16, 2025, and every version up to 4.5 had converted by August 2026.

choices.choice: No server: clients talk to storage directly
choices.why: Pulling compressed data straight from object storage means there is no server to run or overload, and capacity scales with the bucket. The cost is no transactions: writers to the same symbol must coordinate themselves.
Research and backtests need data as it was on a given day. Writing new versions instead of updating in place gives point-in-time reads, and a version once written can’t be corrupted by later updates.

choices.choice: Tile frames by rows and columns
choices.why: Man’s data is wide as well as long, such as modelling a whole corporate bond universe, so segments are cut in both directions and a read can fetch a date range of just a few columns.
The users are quants in Jupyter and pandas. Man’s CTO Gary Collier argued that DataFrames emerge as the unit of analysis in modern data science, and ArcticDB makes them a first-class concern.

timeline.text: Man Group starts Arctic, a pandas datastore on MongoDB
Arctic is open-sourced on GitHub under the LGPL
Ground-up rewrite begins: a C++ engine on S3, without MongoDB
Bloomberg agreement in February; ArcticDB 1.0 under BSL 1.1 in March
ArcticDB 1.0 converts to Apache 2.0, two years after release
6.x releases; every version up to 4.5 is now Apache 2.0
